title: A description of the FAMOUS (version XDBUA) climate model and control run
abstract: Abstract. FAMOUS is an ocean-atmosphere general circulation model of low resolution, capable of simulating approximately 120 years of model climate per wallclock day using current high performance computing facilities. It uses most of the same code as HadCM3, a widely used climate model of higher resolution and computational cost, and has been tuned to reproduce the same climate reasonably well. FAMOUS is useful for climate simulations where the computational cost makes the application of HadCM3 unfeasible, either because of the length of simulation or the size of the ensemble desired. We document a number of scientific and technical improvements to the original version of FAMOUS. These improvements include changes to the parameterisations of ozone and sea-ice which alleviate a significant cold bias from high northern latitudes and the upper troposphere, and the elimination of volume-averaged drifts in ocean tracers. A simple model of the marine carbon cycle has also been included. A particular goal of FAMOUS is to conduct millennial-scale paleoclimate simulations of Quaternary ice ages; to this end, a number of useful changes to the model infrastructure have been made.
problem: High-resolution climate models are too computationally expensive for long-term simulations, while the previous version of the fast FAMOUS model had significant cold biases and non-conservation of ocean tracers, which the improvements described in the paper aim to correct.
method: This paper documents improvements to the FAMOUS climate model, including new parameterizations for ozone and sea-ice and elimination of ocean tracer drift, to alleviate significant cold biases and improve stability for long-timescale climate simulations.
task: The task is to document the scientific and technical improvements in the FAMOUS (version XDBUA) climate model, an efficient, low-resolution version of HadCM3, and to describe and evaluate its performance using a control run simulation.

This paper describes improvements to both the climate and technical infrastructure of FAMOUS contained in the current version, XDBUA. A general overview of FAMOUS is given in Sect. 2, with a more detailed description of the changes since ADTAN in Sect. 3.

The atmosphere component is the Hadley Centre atmosphere model (HadAM3), a quasi-hydrostatic, primitive equation gridpoint model with a hybrid vertical coordinate (see Pope et al., 2000, for full details). It uses an Eulerian advection scheme, with a gravity-wave drag parameterisation (Gregory et al., 1998).

The atmosphere component is the Hadley Centre atmosphere model (HadAM3), a quasi-hydrostatic, primitive equation gridpoint model with a hybrid vertical coordinate (see Pope et al., 2000, for full details). It uses an Eulerian advection scheme, with a gravity-wave drag parameterisation (Gregory et al., 1998).

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Convection follows the mass-flux scheme of Gregory and Rowntree (1990), with parameterisations of convective downdrafts (Gregory and Allen, 1991) and momentum transport (Gregory et al., 1997).
Convection follows the mass-flux scheme of Gregory and Rowntree (1990), with parameterisations of convective downdrafts (Gregory and Allen, 1991) and momentum transport (Gregory et al., 1997).
Land processes are modelled via the Met Office Surface Exchange Scheme (MOSES1) (Cox et al., 1999) land surface scheme.

Since the resolution of the ocean model is greater than the atmosphere, FAMOUS uses a coastal tiling scheme which combines the properties of land and sea in coastal grid boxes in the atmosphere model.
The ocean model is the Hadley Centre ocean model (HadOM3) (see Gordon et al., 2000 for more details), based on the widely used Bryan and Cox code (Bryan, 1969; Cox, 1984).

The ocean model is the Hadley Centre ocean model (HadOM3) (see Gordon et al., 2000 for more details), based on the widely used Bryan and Cox code (Bryan, 1969; Cox, 1984). It is a rigid lid model, where surface freshwater fluxes are converted to virtual tracer fluxes via local surface tracer values (Pardaens et al., 2003).
Temperature and salinity are advected via a simple centred difference method. This has been found to produce better results than more complex schemes at climate model resolutions in HadOM3.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: We use versions of the Gent and McWilliams (1990) and Redi (1982) isopycnal horizontal mixing schemes, with the surface mixed layer of Kraus and Turner (1967).

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: Pacanowski and Philander (1981) Richardson-number dependent scheme
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Diapycnal mixing below the mixed layer is parameterised using the Richardson-number dependent scheme of Pacanowski and Philander (1981).
Convection is modelled via the scheme of Rahmstorf (1993), with Roether et al. (1994) convection being used for additional accuracy in the region of the Greenland-Scotland overflows.
The sea-ice model uses simple, zero-layer thermodynamics (Semtner, 1976), with dynamics based on Bryan (1969).
The sea-ice model uses simple, zero-layer thermodynamics (Semtner, 1976), with dynamics based on Bryan (1969).

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: Cattle and Crossley (1995) ice-drifting and leads parameterisation
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Ice-drifting and leads are parameterised according to Cattle and Crossley (1995).
HadOM3 includes the Hadley Centre ocean carbon model (HadOCC), a simple NPZD (Nutrient, Phytoplankton, Zooplankton, Detritus) model of marine biogeochemistry (Palmer and Totterdell, 2001).

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: simplified parameterisations of light penetration and self shading
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: In FAMOUS, HadOCC uses simplified parameterisations of light penetration and self shading (C. Jones, personal communication, 2007), which differ from the original schemes of Palmer and Totterdell (2001).

Advection of biogeochemical tracers in XDBUA is done using a flux-limited form of the third-order UTOPIA advection scheme (Leonard et al., 1993), which greatly improves the distribution of carbon in the ocean and the resultant exchange of carbon dioxide (CO2) with the atmosphere.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: FAMOUS has a horizontal resolution of 3.75° longitude×2.5° latitude in the ocean, with 20 vertical levels.

At this resolution, outflow from the Mediterranean is parameterised by simple mixing between an area in the Atlantic and one in the Mediterranean from the surface to a depth of 1300 m.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: An artificial island is used at the North Pole to avoid the problem of converging meridians, and Fourier filtering is applied at high latitudes to smooth instabilities caused by the long timestep.

To alleviate this problem, and provide a crude parameterisation of iceberg calving, an additional surface water flux field has been designed (Fig. 2).

In XDBUA therefore, a small, time-dependent, volume-uniform adjustment is added to each of the tracer fields (salinity, alkalinity and dissolved inorganic carbon) to ensure that the global volume integral concentration of each tracer are conserved.
ADTAN suffered from a cold bias at high northern latitudes, accompanied by excessive sea-ice (Jones, 2003; Jones et al., 2005).

Sea-ice albedo in HadCM3 and FAMOUS is temperature dependent, changing linearly between a low “melting” ice albedo (ALPHAM) and a higher “cold” ice albedo (ALPHAC) as overlying air temperatures vary between 0 and −10◦C.
Jones et al. (2005) ran integrations with an atmospheric pCO2 of 580 ppmv (twice the control value) and found α=0.89±0.07W/m²/K for ADTAN, compared to 1.32±0.08 for HadCM3.

An integration of XDBUA using an atmospheric pCO2 of 1160 ppmv found α=1.10±0.09 W/m²/K. Following the usual assumption that α is largely independent of CO2 forcing, the climate sensitivity of XDBUA has thus been moved closer to that of HadCM3.

To avoid this problem, a simple ozone parameterisation was adopted in ADTAN which specified an ozone concentration purely based on whether the gridbox was below, at, or above the diagnosed tropopause (Table 2).

High-altitude temperatures have been improved in XDBUA by the use of a 4-level parameterisation, where, in addition to the 3 categories above, concentrations in the top model level are set to 1.5×10−6 kg/kg, regardless of the height of the tropopause (Table 2).
A control run of XDBUA with a constant atmospheric pCO2 of 290 ppmv (representing the year 1860) has been run for 4000 years.

In the global average, XDBUA has drifted 0.8◦ K further away from HadCM3 than ADTAN, but has replaced ADTAN’s −0.4◦ K cold bias with respect to observations with a 0.4◦ warm bias.

kg_extraction_triplets.target_entity_instance: leading EOF explaining 21% of the total MSLP variability
kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: XDBUA reproduces the basic features of the tripole of Pacific, Arctic and North Atlantic pressure variations seen in observations and HadCM3 (Fig. 9), with the leading EOF explaining 21% of the total MSLP variability in XDBUA.

FAMOUS reproduces the meridional energy transports of HadCM3 relatively well (Fig. 11). Atmospheric energy transports are underestimated by around 0.5 PW at their peak in the midlatitudes, most likely due to the lack of midlatitude variability in FAMOUS.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Peak meridional ocean heat transport in the ocean in FAMOUS is about 0.3 PW less than that in HadCM3, with most of this underestimate being found in the Atlantic MOC.
The Atlantic MOC has a mean of 17 Sv and a decadal standard deviation of 0.83 Sv.
